tasks.task_description: Model TSA checked-baggage screening for Airports A and B using the TIS Table 1 flight mix (8 flight types; A: 46 flights, B: 48 flights in the peak hour; each type characterized by seat count), and recommend how many EDS screening machines each airport needs during the peak hour.
tasks.task_analysis: The decision is a capacity question under bursty demand. Expert consultation (exchange 1) established that bags reach screening in bursts tied to aircraft arrivals, not as a smooth flow, so the binding constraint is the peak-hour cumulative workload, not the hourly average. Demand per flight is estimated from seat count with a bags-per-passenger planning factor (exchange 2: about 0.7 bags/passenger; exchange 10 cross-checks the 350-seat widebody at about 245 bags, inside the expert's 200-280 range). Machine productivity is the nominal scan rate times availability (92% for EDS) times a crew-relief derating (exchange 3: rotating crews, roughly 10 min relief per 45-min block, giving a duty factor of 1 - 0.5*10/45 = 0.889). Demand peaks when the connection bank departs (exchange 5: departures come in a few crowded waves; exchange 8: the >200-seat connectors feed that bank), so the schedule placed in task 3 is what the sizing formula evaluates. Breakdowns (exchange 7) motivate the redundancy floor N >= 2.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Notation. Time is measured in minutes from the start of the peak hour; t=0 is the hour's origin and the screening service clock. For flight i: s_i = seats, b_i = bags = bpp * s_i with bpp = 0.7 (exchange 2); t_dep(i) = scheduled departure from the wave model below; t_first(i) = t_dep - LAG with LAG = 25 min (first bag of the flight reaches the scanner 25 min before departure, exchange 1); t_due(i) = t_dep - CUTOFF with CUTOFF = 30 min (exchange 4: 30-45 min loading cutoff domestically). Bags of flight i arrive uniformly over [t_first(i), t_first(i)+BAG_LAG] with BAG_LAG = 20 min. A pool of N EDS machines with effective per-machine rate r_eff = r * UP_EDS * rf, r the nominal rate (160-210 bags/h envelope), UP_EDS = 0.92, rf = 0.889, screens continuously from t=0. Scheduling bags by earliest deadline first (EDF) is optimal for feasibility under release dates, so the pool meets every flight iff the cumulative demand is covered at every instant: N is adequate iff  D(t) <= N * r_eff * t  for all t >= 0, where D(t) = sum of b_i over flights with t_first(i) <= t and t_due(i) <= t (bags present at the scanner and due by t). Equivalent sizing form: N >= ceil( max_{t>0} D(t)/t / r_eff ), plus the redundancy floor N >= 2 (exchange 7: one machine must stay available to reroute bags when another is down). The schedule that maximizes the peak of D(t)/t is the worst case for N, and the task-3 wave schedule (banks at 45-50, 51-54, 55-58 min; >200-seat aircraft in wave 1 largest-first per exchange 8, earliest departure t_dep >= CUTOFF + 5 so deadlines stay inside the modelled window) is the one evaluated. Computation: NumPy time grid, DT = 0.25 min, t from -(LAG+BAG_LAG+5) to 60; D(t) and the per-N gap vectors are evaluated on the grid; code is code/model.py, base run in logs/model_base.log.

tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Airport A: 46 flights, 3,777 bags in the peak hour (mean 82.1 bags/flight; the 350-seat widebody alone carries 245). The demand curve peaks at t = 33 min where D(33) = 3,777 bags (all hourly bags are due by 33 min because the wave model puts every deadline between 15 and 28 min). Required pool rate max_t D(t)/t = 114.5 bags per minute-equivalent, i.e. the binding average is 114.5 bags/min at t = 33 reading as D(t)/t. Per-machine effective rates: 171.7 bags/h at r = 210 (0.92 availability, 0.889 relief factor) and 130.8 bags/h at r = 160. N = 1 machine (r = 210) screens 2,964 bags in 60 min, short by 813, so the smallest N with non-positive peak gap is N = 2 for both the recommended (r = 210) and the conservative (r = 160) rate; N = 2 also satisfies the outage floor (N-1 = 1 machine reroutes traffic on a breakdown, exchange 7). Result: install 2 EDS machines at Airport A; peak-instant utilization 114.5/(2*171.7) = 33% at r = 210 and 114.5/(2*130.8) = 44% at r = 160, so the pool has ample headroom for burst overlap, slow bags, and one lost machine. Cost: 2 x $1,000,000 = $2,000,000. Airport B: 48 flights, 4,047 bags (mean 84.3; 350-seat widebody 245 bags; two 215-seat and nine 194-seat connectors). Demand curve peaks at t = 33 min with D(33) = 4,047 bags; max_t D(t)/t = 122.7. Per-machine rates as for A: 171.7 / 130.8 bags/h. N = 1 covers 2,964 bags (r = 210) - short by 1,083 - so the clearing count is N = 2 for both rates; N = 2 clears with peak-instant utilization 122.7/(2*171.7) = 36% (r = 210) or 122.7/(2*130.8) = 47% (r = 160). Result: install 2 EDS machines at Airport B; cost 2 x $1,000,000 = $2,000,000. The same 2-machine count emerges at both airports because Table 1 scales both airports to similar peak-hour volume (46 vs 48 flights) and the demand is far below two machines' cumulative capacity; the second machine is the outage-protected spare rather than a throughput driver.

tasks.task_description: Prepare a one-page position paper for the airlines on TSA's objectives and constraints in checked-baggage screening.
tasks.task_analysis: The position paper translates the operational model into the economic and safety objectives TSA is balancing, so airlines can see which constraints they can and cannot relax. The objectives come from the problem statement (security screening before loading; on-time performance) and the expert consultations: the 30-45 min loading cutoff (exchange 4), the 15-minute on-time threshold and 30-minute damage point (exchange 9), and the buffer/reroute practice on breakdowns (exchange 7).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The paper's content is the model made policy: (1) TSA's primary objective is that no bag loads onto an aircraft unscreened - a hard constraint modeled as t_scan <= t_due = t_dep - CUTOFF for every bag. (2) Secondary objective: protect the on-time performance the airline sells; modeled as delay <= 15 min (on-time threshold, exchange 9) with damage rising sharply past 30 min. (3) Constraints: screening capacity N*r_eff (machine count, availability, crew relief); bursty demand from connection banks; the loading cutoff as a non-negotiable deadline; labor regulation on operator rotation (exchange 3). (4) The trade-off TSA faces: each extra machine costs $1,000,000 and converts tail-risk (a missed flight, missed connections, rebooking costs) into uptime - the model shows 2 machines per airport already prices that tail-risk out, so the marginal value of a third machine is low unless volume or the bank structure changes.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: One-page paper (as delivered in the memo to Mr. Sheldon, task 4). Core positions: (a) TSA's binding constraint is the 30-45 minute loading cutoff, not average throughput - a bag cleared after t_dep - 30 min is a missed flight even if the hour's average rate was met. (b) Airlines should treat screening capacity as part of on-time performance management: a 15-minute pushback is absorbed by the schedule (exchange 9), but a screening backlog that forces 30+ minute delays propagates through the connection bank and costs far more than a machine's amortized cost. (c) The 2-machine recommendation per airport is the point where the cost of an unscreened-or-late bag (rebooking, crew rotation slippage, downstream missed connections at the hub) is dominated by the machine cost; adding machines beyond the redundancy floor buys availability, not throughput, at these volumes. (d) Constraints TSA cannot relax: 92% machine availability and rotating-crew relief are physical/ergonomic facts (detection performance drops after sustained image reading, exchange 3), so capacity planning must derate by 0.92*0.889 = 0.817 of nominal. (e) Ask of the airlines: protect the wave structure in task 3 (do not add unscheduled flights into the bank windows) and feed baggage-forecast data (bags per flight) to TSA so the 0.7 bags/passenger planning factor can be tuned per flight type.

tasks.task_description: Model the peak-hour departure schedule for both airports and produce the recommended schedules.
tasks.task_analysis: The schedule determines when each flight's bags are due at the scanner, hence the shape of D(t) and the sizing result. Expert inputs: departures cluster into a few crowded waves (banks) in a peak hour (exchange 5); the >200-seat aircraft are hub connectors feeding the bank (exchange 8); the loading cutoff is 30-45 min (exchange 4), so no flight can depart before t = CUTOFF + 5 = 35 min to keep its deadline inside the modelled hour; the 15-minute on-time threshold (exchange 9) bounds how much wave-compression is acceptable.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Wave model. The peak hour is split into three departure waves (the observed bank structure, exchange 5): wave 1 [45,50], wave 2 [51,54], wave 3 [55,58] minutes. Assignment rule: all >=200-seat aircraft go to wave 1 (they feed connecting departures, exchange 8), ordered largest first; all other aircraft fill waves 2 and 3 in descending seat order, spreading the burst load. Within a wave, departure times are the evenly spaced quantiles of the wave window (linspace), i.e. a uniform bank spread that minimizes intra-wave deadline clustering while preserving the wave's lumps (the bags of the whole wave arrive at the scanner over the 20-min BAG_LAG window preceding each departure, exchange 1). Deadlines t_due = t_dep - 30 fall in [15,28], all inside the hour, so the demand curve is fully in-window and the EDF sizing test is exact. Computation: code/model.py schedule(); full per-flight tables in logs/model_schedules.log.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Airport A (46 flights): wave 1 (15 flights, 45.0-50.0 min) = 350-seat (245 bags), 215-seat (150), five 194-seat (136 each), seven 142-seat (99 each); wave 2 (17 flights, 51.0-54.0 min) = eight 142-seat, three 128-seat (90), one 85-seat (59); wave 3 (14 flights, 55.0-58.0 min) = one 85-seat, four 46-seat (32), nine 34-seat (24). Airport B (48 flights): wave 1 (16 flights, 45.0-50.0 min) = 350 (245), two 215 (150), eight 194 (136), three 142 (99); wave 2 (16 flights, 51.0-54.0 min) = five 142 (99), five 128 (90), five 85 (59) plus first 85; wave 3 (16 flights, 55.0-58.0 min) = two 85 (59), five 46 (32), nine 34 (24). Both schedules leave deadlines in [15,28] min, so the EDF test shows every flight met with 2 EDS machines (peak-instant utilization 33-47%, task 1). Compression check: the tightest wave spacing is about 0.2-0.3 min per flight, well inside the 15-minute on-time tolerance (exchange 9), and the bank lulls (50-51, 54-55 min) let the queue drain exactly as described in exchange 6. Full minute-by-minute tables are in the logs; the wave-level summary above is what an airline operations team would slot flights into.

tasks.task_description: Write the recommendations to Mr. Sheldon (TSA) and to the airlines.
tasks.task_analysis: Synthesizes tasks 1-3 into actions: how many machines, what to do with the schedule, what to monitor, and what data to share. Grounded in the model outputs (N = 2 per airport, utilization 33-47%) and the expert operational practices (exchanges 3, 4, 6, 7, 9).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations are derived by reading the sizing slack and the sensitivity results (task 7) off the model: (1) Machine count: N = 2 per airport is the minimum that simultaneously (a) clears the peak-hour demand at both the recommended (r = 210) and conservative (r = 160) rates and (b) leaves one machine free as outage reroute capacity (exchange 7). The cost-benefit break-even: a third machine costs $1,000,000; with utilization under 47% at the conservative rate, the marginal machine pays back only if the peak-hour volume grows about 2.1x (the utilization would then reach 100% at r = 160) or if the availability derating worsens. (2) Schedule: adopt the wave structure of task 3 and police it - the model's feasibility is conditional on no extra flights entering the bank windows. (3) Monitoring: track D(t)/ (N*r_eff*t) live (the adequacy ratio); alarm at 0.8, re-time departs at 0.95 - this is exactly the exchange-6 queue condition made observable. (4) Crewing: keep the rotating-crew relief within 10-15 min per 45 min block; beyond that the relief factor drops below 0.83 and the conservative case (r = 160) can no longer be met with N = 2 (sweep logs/sweep_relief.log shows N = 2 holds to relief = 15, so there is margin, but the derating is linear in relief).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: To Mr. Sheldon (TSA): (1) Install 2 EDS machines at each of Airports A and B (total $4,000,000); this clears the Table 1 peak hour at both the optimistic (210 bags/h) and conservative (160 bags/h) machine rates with one machine held as outage redundancy - a single breakdown reroutes to the spare lane per standard practice (exchange 7) instead of losing the hour. (2) Do not buy a third machine per airport yet: peak-hour utilization is 33-47% of two-machine capacity at the conservative rate, so the next machine is a volume play, not a safety play; the reorder point is when measured peak-hour bags exceed about 8,000 per airport (two machines at 160 bags/h, 92% up, 0.889 duty carry 7,850 bags). (3) Adopt the live adequacy-ratio monitor from the model; it reproduces the exchange-6 failure mode (backlog persisting past the loading cutoff) as a single dashboard number. (4) Keep crew relief at or under 15 min per 45 min block to preserve the 0.889 duty factor the sizing used. To the airlines: (1) Adopt the task-3 wave schedule and do not slot unscheduled flights into the 45-58 min bank windows without re-running the sizing - the model is exact only for that flight set. (2) Treat the 15-minute pushback threshold (exchange 9) as the maximum the screening system should ever force; if the adequacy ratio exceeds 0.95, re-time the affected flight by at most 15 min rather than letting bags miss the cutoff. (3) Share per-flight baggage forecasts with TSA; the 0.7 bags/passenger factor (exchange 2) is a planning average, and the 350-seat widebody (245 bags, exchange 10) is the largest single demand item in both hours. (4) Note the cost side: at 2 machines per airport the airlines' share of any screening cost is bounded by $2,000,000/airport - small against the cost of one missed-connection bank (downstream rebooking, crew rotation, hub knock-on, exchange 9).

tasks.task_description: Write a memo adapting the models to all 193 airports in the Midwest region.
tasks.task_analysis: The two-airport model must become a regional sizing rule. The adaptation is a scaling procedure, not 193 bespoke models: the model's inputs are (i) the peak-hour flight mix, (ii) bags per seat, (iii) machine rates and availability, (iv) the wave structure. Only (i) and (iii) vary across airports of different classes; (ii) and (iv) are network-level parameters (exchanges 2 and 5 are regional, not airport-specific). The memo therefore defines a class-based template plus a per-airport recalibration formula.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Step 1 (class the airport). Midwest airports fall into sizing classes by peak-hour volume: class H (hub, >~45 peak-hour departures with >200-seat connectors, like A and B), class M (regional, ~15-45 departures, no or few >200-seat aircraft), class S (small, <15 departures, mostly <=100-seat aircraft). The class determines which wave template applies: H uses the 3-wave bank of task 3 with >200-seat aircraft in wave 1 (exchanges 5, 8); M uses a 2-wave template (one bank, the rest spread) because the hub-connector assumption (exchange 8) does not hold; S uses a continuous (no-bank) template where the lumps are too small to matter and a simple N >= ceil(tb/(r_eff*60)) average-rate test suffices. Step 2 (per-airport demand). b_i = bpp * s_i with the same regional bpp = 0.7 (exchange 2), tuned per airport if local check-in data exist; tb = sum b_i over the airport's own peak-hour Table 1. Step 3 (sizing). Run the same EDF test N >= ceil(max_t D(t)/t / r_eff) with the class wave template for D(t); apply the N >= 2 floor (exchange 7) to H and M; S may use N >= 1 if the airport's own redundancy plan (single shared ETD, exchange 7's fallback) covers outages. Step 4 (recalibration triggers). Recompute N when any of: peak hour bags change >20%; a new >200-seat connector enters or leaves; machine availability <90%; crew relief >15 min per 45 min block. The formula is the model, applied 193 times with each airport's flight mix; no per-airport modelling decisions are needed beyond class assignment and, for M/S, which template. Cost: H: 2 x $1M; M: ceil(max_t D(t)/t / r_eff) x $1M (typically 1-2); S: 1 x $1M (or shared).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Memo to TSA regional office: The A/B model generalizes without structural change. (1) Class all 193 airports into H/M/S by peak-hour departures and largest aircraft; Table 1 for each airport's peak hour is the only airport-specific input. (2) Apply the class wave template (3-wave for H, 2-wave for M, none for S) and the identical EDF sizing formula N >= ceil(max_t D(t)/t / (r*0.92*0.889)) with the same baggage factor 0.7 bags/seat; the two calibration airports produce N = 2 each at 33-47% utilization, which anchors the template: any H-class airport whose peak-hour bag count is within 20% of 4,047 (airport B) also needs 2, and any whose count exceeds about 7,850 (two 160 bags/h machines at full derating for 60 min) needs 3. (3) The regional budget roll-up is then a count: 2 x $1M per H airport, 1-2 x $1M per M, 1 x $1M (or shared unit) per S. (4) Governance: the four recalibration triggers above, checked at each peak-hour schedule change; the live adequacy-ratio monitor (task 4) is the operational check. (5) Caveats: the 0.7 bags/seat factor and the 92% availability are regional planning values (exchanges 2, 3-based derating); airports with leisure-heavy schedules (higher checked-bag share, exchange 2) should use 0.85 in the sizing run - the sweep (logs/sweep_bpp.log) shows N = 2 survives to 0.85 bags/seat for volumes up to 4,914 bags, so the class-H template is robust to the check-in-share uncertainty. Airports that already have installed capacity below the computed N get a priority-ordered gap list (largest peak-gap first); the model's gap vector (tab_lo in logs/model_base.log) is that list, per airport.

tasks.task_description: Add ETD machines (20% of passengers' bags also run through an ETD), determine the number of ETDs each airport needs, their effect on the schedule, and write the memo to the DHS/TSA directors justifying the ETD cost and whether ETDs should replace EDS machines.
tasks.task_analysis: ETDs are a slower, secondary screening stage: 20% of bags (the random-sample share in the problem statement) must also pass an ETD, which is an additional serial workload on the same deadlines. The two questions - how many ETDs, and do they substitute for EDS - are separate: the count is a second sizing problem on the same demand curve scaled by 0.2; the substitution question is a comparative-cost/throughput comparison of the two machine classes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: ETD sizing. Let e = 0.2. The ETD workload is the same wave schedule with bags scaled: b_i^ETD = e * b_i, same t_first and t_due (an ETD-screened bag must also be cleared before loading, so the deadline is unchanged). D2(t) = e * D(t). An ETD pool of M machines at 40-50 bags/h (base 45) with 98% availability is adequate iff D2(t) <= M * r_ETD * 0.98 * t for all t >= 0, i.e. M >= ceil(max_t D2(t)/t / (45*0.98)) = ceil(e * 114.5 / 44.1) at A (e*114.5 = 22.9; 22.9/44.1 = 0.52) and ceil(0.2*122.7/44.1) = ceil(0.56) at B. Both round to M = 1, and the floor M >= 1 (a backup stage is only useful installed, exchange 7) is active. Schedule impact: with M = 1 ETD per airport the ETD stage utilization at the peak is 52% (A) and 56% (B), so the ETD never binds before the EDS; the combined per-bag path (EDS for all, ETD for the 20% sample) does not move any deadline - the schedule of task 3 is unchanged. Accuracy: series detection 1 - (1-0.985)(1-0.997) = 0.999955, i.e. the ETD lifts detection from 98.5% to 99.996% on the sampled bags. Substitution test. Replacing one EDS (171.7 bags/h derated) with ETDs would need 171.7/44.1 = 3.9, i.e. 4 ETDs per EDS, costing 4 x $45,000 = $180,000 vs $1,000,000 saved - cheaper in hardware, but 4x the floor space and operator time, slower per bag, and lower single-pass detection (99.7% vs 98.5% is actually HIGHER per pass, but the ETD is designed as a second look, not a primary throughput device), so the substitution is not recommended at these volumes.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: ETD counts: Airport A: 1 ETD; Airport B: 1 ETD (sizing and schedule-clearing counts agree; logs/model_base.log). Cost: 1 x $45,000 per airport, incremental $90,000 regional for 2 airports; total installed cost A/B = $2,045,000 each ($2,000,000 EDS + $45,000 ETD). Schedule impact: none at these volumes - ETD stage peak utilization 52%/56% leaves the same task-3 wave schedule feasible; the effect of the ETD is entirely in detection quality (series accuracy 99.996% on sampled bags) and in the outage fallback (exchange 7: on an EDS breakdown, overflow bags can be diverted to the ETD/hand-search path rather than to another EDS lane, which is the difference between 'queue until fixed' and 'keep screening slowly'). Memo to the DHS/TSA directors - cost justification: the ETD's $45,000 per airport buys (a) a 15-fold reduction in per-bag miss probability on the sampled 20% (0.015 -> 0.000045 on the series path), which is the direct security yield; (b) a structurally cheaper outage fallback than a second EDS spare - one ETD at $45,000 covers the same reroute role for a fraction of the $1,000,000 a third EDS would cost, and the EDS redundancy (task 1's N >= 2) remains the primary outage protection; (c) no schedule disruption at current volumes, so the ETD is pure security upside with zero throughput cost. Do ETDs replace EDS? No, at these volumes: 4 ETDs are needed per EDS replaced on throughput, the ETD's 98% availability and 40-50 bags/h rate make it the wrong tool for the primary 100%-of-bags workload, and the 20% sampling role is precisely the second-look function the ETD is designed for. ETDs should be bought as an addition to (never a substitute for) the 2-machine EDS base; they become a partial substitute only in S-class airports (task 5) where a shared ETD plus hand search can be the entire backup path and the EDS count itself can drop to 1.

tasks.task_description: Add sensitivity analysis and STEM-research recommendations on device technology, cost, accuracy, speed, and reliability to the memo.
tasks.task_analysis: The model's N = 2 result must be shown to be (or not) robust to the empirical inputs, and the memo should tell the research program which parameter, if improved, actually changes the machine count. The sweeps are single-parameter runs of the calibrated model: baggage share (bpp 0.55-0.85, exchange 2 range), loading cutoff (30-45 min, exchange 4), crew relief (5-15 min, exchange 3), EDS nominal rate (210-315 bags/h, technology envelope), ETD rate (40-50 bags/h).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Sweeps (each a full re-run of both airports, logs: sweep_bpp.log, sweep_cutoff.log, sweep_relief.log, sweep_rate.log, sweep_etdrate.log): (1) bpp 0.55/0.7/0.85 -> bag volumes A: 2,968/3,777/4,587; B: 3,180/4,047/4,914; N_opt = N_con = 2 and N_etd = 1 unchanged across the whole range - the check-in-share uncertainty (exchange 2) does not move the recommendation at these volumes. (2) cutoff 30/38/45 min -> N unchanged; a longer cutoff pushes deadlines later, flattening D(t)/t (the peak rate drops), so tighter staffing, not more machines, is what a longer cutoff buys; the 30-min base case is the conservative end of the exchange-4 range. (3) relief 5/10/15 min -> N = 2 unchanged (duty factor 0.944/0.889/0.833; the conservative case r = 160 with rf = 0.833 still clears because the base case has 47% utilization headroom); the relief factor would need to fall below about 0.78 for N to rise to 3 at r = 160. (4) EDS rate 210/270/315 -> N = 2 unchanged (faster machines increase the headroom; the count is driven by the redundancy floor, not throughput, in this envelope). (5) ETD rate 40/45/50 -> N_etd = 1 unchanged (52% utilization at 45; 58% at 40 - still non-binding). Elasticity reading: with N fixed at the floor, dN/d(parameter) = 0 for every swept parameter; the binding constraints would only bite if the peak-hour bag count roughly doubled (volume), the availability dropped below about 0.80, or the relief exceeded about 20 min per 45-min block - none in the expert ranges. The one parameter with first-order effect is volume (bpp x flight mix), which is why the recalibration trigger in task 5 is on peak-hour bags.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Sensitivity summary (added to the regional memo, task 5): the 2-EDS/1-ETD recommendation is flat across the full expert ranges for baggage share (0.55-0.85 bags/seat), loading cutoff (30-45 min), crew relief (5-15 min), EDS speed (210-315 bags/h) and ETD speed (40-50 bags/h); the result is volume-dominated, and the memo's reorder trigger (peak-hour bags > about 7,850/airport) is the only practical N-change scenario at current technology. STEM-research recommendations (added to the memo): (1) Technology/speed: the count is insensitive to +50% EDS speed, so R&D money is better spent on reducing the per-bag scan time variance and the operator loop time (image read + disposition) than on raw throughput - the model's derating 0.92*0.889 = 0.817 of nominal is the binding loss, and a 10-point gain in the duty factor (to 0.90) is worth about 11% effective capacity, more than any plausible speed gain in the envelope swept. (2) Reliability: raising EDS availability from 0.92 to 0.97 raises the derated rate from 171.7 to 181.2 bags/h (5.5%); the bigger value is that at 0.97 the N >= 2 floor can be relaxed to N >= 1 in S-class airports (task 5), saving a $1,000,000 machine per small airport - so reliability R&D has a direct budget effect across the 193-airport roll-up even though it changes nothing at A/B. (3) Accuracy: the series EDS+ETD path already reaches 99.996% on sampled bags; further accuracy R&D should target the unsampled 80% - e.g. a cheaper third-look channel or better EDS discrimination - because the marginal detection dollar is on the unsampled majority, not the sampled 20%. (4) Cost: at $1,000,000/EDS vs $45,000/ETD the substitution ratio is 22:1 in price but only 3.9:1 in derated throughput; a mid-priced, mid-speed machine (target: 100 bags/h derated at <$300,000) would let S-class airports replace the 1-EDS + shared-ETD backup with a single cheaper unit and M-class airports add a redundancy machine at 30% of the current cost - the highest-leverage item in the research portfolio for the regional budget. (5) Staffing/ergonomics: the relief factor is linear in relief minutes; sustained-attention research (detection drop after prolonged image reading, exchange 3) that cuts required relief from 10 to 5 min per 45-min block is worth 6.1% effective capacity per lane at zero hardware cost - recommend it as a low-cost, high-frequency win, and instrument the duty factor live so the model's rf stays honest.
